rv.q: The whole enterprise is both unbearably moving and surprisingly funny.
So much goes right in this exceptional production that it's quite simply a killer Mockingbird.
Aaron Sorkin finds effective ways in his confident adaptation, drawing out the lawyer’s moral inconsistencies without undermining his goodness completely.
Otherwise, this is a tremendously effective adaptation that not only does justice to the original but, where it matters most, improves upon it.

Hats off to Aaron Sorkin. While the official title may be Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, this captivating drama is very much Sorkin's take on a story that has become embedded in the consciousness of generations of readers.
Breathing fresh life into one of the most famous characters of all time is no small achievement: this ambivalent Atticus is a huge achievement for both Sorkin and Spall.
Nevertheless, this is a thin, often awkward evening. More of an argument than an experience.
Spall's great achievement is to locate a rumpled, creased authority within a potentially saintly character who is rescued here from unimpeachable rectitude.
The perceptiveness of such thoughts is what makes the show much more than a courtroom drama with a subplot about a lawyer's family life.
It's impossible not to be swept along by this nimble-footed play, which offers a lot of laughs to lighten the gloom of its post-Depression realities.
That's an odd failing for a play about ethics.
Aaron Sorkin's To Kill a Mockingbird is powerful, moving, and brimming with humour; a magnificently awe-inspiring piece of theatre.
